paras: The Coal Valley strike and Black replacement miners episode was a confrontation in November 1881 in Fayette County, West Virginia, in which striking coal miners at Coal Valley drove off the first group of Black miners brought from Virginia to take their places. When a second group arrived, county authorities called for troops, and two militia companies guarded the new men until the strikers dispersed. Accounts in the Wheeling Register differed on whether the strikers used threats: a visiting correspondent said they stopped "short of violence," while the county prosecutor said they threatened the men's lives.

About 500 men in the soft-coal mines at Coal Valley were on strike for an advance of fifteen cents over the sixty-two and a half cents per ton they were paid. The operators said they could not pay it unless the C. & O. railroad raised the ninety-five cents per ton it paid them for coal, and the miners said they could not live on the old rate when cars were furnished only half the time. In mid-November the Coal Valley Courier reported that the strike among the gas coal miners continued with "no show for an early adjustment."

In the same weeks, at Cannelton in the Kanawha Valley, strikers forced sixty new men to quit, and the Governor was asked to order out the Kanawha Riflemen and another company. A November 17 telegram to Governor J. B. Jackson reported that the sheriff and prosecuting attorney expected trouble there and that the Hawk's Nest Rifles had been summoned.

According to Fayette prosecuting attorney J. W. St. Clair, the operators at Strain's first offered their former miners work at the old prices and then imported "colored miners." He said the old hands "got the first set of negroes imported to stop, by threatening their lives," while offering to take care of them if they quit. Women assembled at the pitmouth with pans and sticks as several hundred men gathered nearby, and some of the new hands crawled out through the air-course rather than face the crowd.

When a second group of Black miners was brought in, about 400 strikers waited for them at the station. Sheriff Tyree, saying the county officials could not protect the new hands, obtained the Governor's permission to call on the militia. Two companies guarded the Black miners for a couple of days, until the strikers saw they could not drive them out and dispersed.

No report of arrests, indictments or a trial arising from the confrontation was found in the coverage. St. Clair said trespassers could not be punished under existing law and that the miners' union kept witnesses from testifying, and he called for legislation like that which had ended similar troubles in Pennsylvania. In the same interview St. Clair mentioned "the day I shot the negro who was endeavoring to escape," but gave no date, place or name.

Only West Virginia white papers covered the strike, and the Wheeling Register carried both detailed accounts of the clash with the Black miners. Its correspondent, who went to the scene after "alarming reports of lawlessness" had been telegraphed to the papers, wrote that the peace was not broken and called the troop call "premature" and "a serious mistake on the part of the Fayette authorities."

Eleven days later the Register printed the prosecutor's account from Washington under subheads such as "Force With Force" and "Were Powerless," letting him defend armed guards and troops. Both accounts called the imported men "negroes," named none of them and gave no version from them, and St. Clair described the second group as "negroes of the same class." Reports on the Cannelton strike, headed "Another Dispatch From the Seat of War" in the Register and closely echoed in the Morgantown New Dominion, printed official telegrams and promised that the Governor would protect the operators in their rights.

The correspondent said the strikers did all they could "short of violence" and that the officers themselves admitted there was no trouble beyond the civil authorities' power. St. Clair, an official defending the call for troops, said instead that the strikers threatened the imported men's lives and that the county officials were powerless.

reader.title: Coal Valley strike and Black replacement miners (1881)
bases: Striking miners turned away Black miners imported as replacements, and troops were called to protect the replacements; no killing or injury of the Black miners is reported (A4, A5).

Two independent Wheeling Register informants, a visiting correspondent and the county prosecutor, agree that strikers stopped the first imported Black miners and that troops were called (A4, A5), though they disagree on whether threats were used.

accounts.label: Visiting correspondent
accounts.gist: Strikers did all they could 'short of violence' to dissuade others; the first batch of Virginia negroes was dissuaded; the peace was not broken and the call for troops was premature.

accounts.label: County prosecutor
accounts.gist: Strikers stopped the first imported negroes by threatening their lives, with women massed at the pitmouth; about 400 met the next group at the station, and two companies had to guard the new men.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Register's correspondent, writing after 'alarming reports of lawlessness,' downplayed the trouble, called the troop call 'a serious mistake' and treated the strike chiefly as a wage dispute caused by the railroad.
The Register's December 14 interview, headed 'Force With Force,' let the prosecutor defend armed guards and troops for the operators and the imported men.
Cannelton reports, headed 'Another Dispatch From the Seat of War,' printed official telegrams and promised the Governor would protect the operators' rights.
